## Proof

Let \(A \in O(n+1) \) be an orthogonal matrix, and define
\[
f_A \colon \mathbb{S}^n \to \mathbb{S}^n, \qquad f_A(x) = Ax.
\]
Since \(A\) is orthogonal, \(f_A\) is a diffeomorphism of \(\mathbb{S}^n\) (with inverse \(f_{A^{-1}}\)). We claim
\[
\deg(f_A) = \det(A).
\]

**Step 1: Reduction via connected components of \(O(n+1)\).**

The group \(O(n+1)\) has two connected components: \(\mathrm{SO}(n+1) = \{A : \det A = +1\}\) and \(\{A : \det A = -1\}\). The degree is a homotopy invariant of maps \(\mathbb{S}^n \to \mathbb{S}^n\). If \(A_t\) is a continuous path in \(O(n+1)\) from \(A_0\) to \(A_1\), then \(f_{A_t}\) gives a homotopy from \(f_{A_0}\) to \(f_{A_1}\), so \(\deg(f_{A_0}) = \deg(f_{A_1})\).

Hence \(\deg(f_A)\) depends only on the connected component of \(A\), i.e., only on \(\operatorname{sgn}(\det A)\). It suffices to compute the degree for one representative of each component: the identity \(I\) (with \(\det = +1\)) and a reflection \(R = \operatorname{diag}(-1, 1, \dots, 1)\) (with \(\det = -1\)).

**Step 2: The identity component.**

For \(A = I\), \(f_A = \mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{S}^n}\), so \(\deg(f_I) = 1 = \det(I)\). By Step 1, every \(A \in \mathrm{SO}(n+1)\) satisfies \(\deg(f_A) = 1 = \det(A)\).

**Step 3: The reflection component — local computation of the degree.**

For a diffeomorphism \(f \colon \mathbb{S}^n \to \mathbb{S}^n\), the degree equals the sign of the Jacobian determinant at any point (the sign is constant since \(f\) is a local diffeomorphism and \(\mathbb{S}^n\) is connected for \(n \geq 1\); for \(n=0\) the result is checked directly).

The standard orientation on \(\mathbb{S}^n \subset \mathbb{R}^{n+1}\) is the **outward-normal-first** convention: a basis \((v_1, \dots, v_n)\) of \(T_x \mathbb{S}^n\) is positively oriented if and only if \((x, v_1, \dots, v_n)\) is a positively oriented basis of \(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\).

The derivative of \(f_A\) at \(x\) is the linear map
\[
(df_A)_x \colon T_x \mathbb{S}^n \to T_{Ax}\mathbb{S}^n, \qquad v \mapsto Av,
\]
since \(T_x \mathbb{S}^n = x^\perp\) and \(A\) maps \(x^\perp\) to \((Ax)^\perp = T_{Ax}\mathbb{S}^n\).

Now take a positively oriented basis \((v_1, \dots, v_n)\) of \(T_x \mathbb{S}^n\), so \((x, v_1, \dots, v_n)\) is positively oriented in \(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\). Applying \(A\),
\[
(x, v_1, \dots, v_n) \;\xmapsto{\;A\;}\; (Ax, Av_1, \dots, Av_n).
\]
The determinant of \(A\) as a linear map on \(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\) is \(\det(A)\), so the oriented \((n+1)\)-tuple \((Ax, Av_1, \dots, Av_n)\) has orientation sign \(\det(A)\) relative to the standard orientation of \(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\). By the outward-normal convention, \((Av_1, \dots, Av_n)\) is a positively oriented basis of \(T_{Ax}\mathbb{S}^n\) if and only if \((Ax, Av_1, \dots, Av_n)\) is positively oriented in \(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\), which happens precisely when \(\det(A) = +1\).

Therefore the Jacobian determinant of \(f_A\) at every point is \(\det(A)\), and since \(f_A\) is a diffeomorphism,
\[
\deg(f_A) = \det(A).
\]

**Step 4: Conclusion.**

For the reflection \(R = \operatorname{diag}(-1, 1, \dots, 1)\), \(\det(R) = -1\), so \(\deg(f_R) = -1\). Every \(A\) with \(\det A = -1\) lies in the same component as \(R\), hence \(\deg(f_A) = -1 = \det(A)\). Combining both components:

\[
\boxed{\deg(f_A) = \det(A) \in \{+1, -1\}.}
\]

### PROOF COMPLETE
